source.title: Dynamic Chunking for End-to-End Hierarchical Sequence Modeling
source.authors: Sukjun Hwang; Brandon Wang; Albert Gu

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some figure content is garbled in the extraction, but the relevant ablation captions and descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests architecture sensitivity of language-model loss through architecture ablations, rather than reproducing a scaling-law fit.
record.gate_note: The authors explicitly say they did not estimate formal scaling-law coefficients or sweep model sizes and compute horizons. Training curves and downstream benchmark results are not evidence of power-law fits or extrapolation, so they are not recorded as rows for V1–V3 or V6. Architecture-ablation results bear on V4. Cited scaling-law results are not rows.
record.test_reason: This is an architecture paper (H-Net, dynamic chunking). It fits no scaling law, sweeps no model sizes and fits no compute-optimal split. The authors state they did not estimate scaling-law coefficients because of resource constraints. It borrows Hoffmann et al.'s FLOP accounting only to match compute across models. The encoder/decoder ablations swap layer types (Mamba-2 vs Transformer) inside a hierarchical byte model. That is a choice of layer family, not the depth/width/shape variation at fixed parameter count that V4 names. Kaplan et al. themselves report that architecture family (e.g. LSTM vs Transformer) matters. The DNA ablation is not language-model pretraining and its parameter counts are not matched (62–66M). So no row bears on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right but misplaced emphasis. The main conclusion is that a byte-level H-Net with learned dynamic chunking beats a compute- and data-matched BPE Transformer. Two-stage H-Nets improve further, with better data scaling, and match a Transformer twice their size downstream. Gains are larger on Chinese, code and DNA. The finding that Mamba encoders/decoders work best is one ablation result. The authors explicitly did not fit formal scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: Architecture ablations measure validation bits-per-byte and perplexity; the study does not fit scaling laws or estimate compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The results vary with encoder-decoder layer composition and input representation (raw bytes versus GPT-2-tokenized input); DNA ablation results also vary slightly across architectures.

fits_no_version.finding: Swapping Mamba-2 for Transformer layers in byte-level H-Net/SpaceByte++ encoders and decoders changes validation BPB substantially. Pure Transformer (T2-T2) is by far worst, and more Mamba layers help monotonically. Mamba layers also help on BPE-tokenized inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At matched parameters, the choice of sequence-mixing layer type in the outer stages of hierarchical byte-level models strongly affects pretraining loss.

fits_no_version.finding: In DNA H-Net, encoder/main-network layer-type variants differ only slightly in final perplexity (2.697–2.722).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In DNA hierarchical models, layer-type composition has small effects on perplexity.

fits_no_version.finding: Under constant-LR phases, H-Net (2-stage) shows steeper loss-vs-data curves than a BPE Transformer. It crosses over at 30B bytes (XL), and achieves ~3.6x data efficiency on DNA. No power law is fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dynamic-chunking hierarchical byte models improve faster with data than tokenized Transformers at fixed compute per byte.

record.problems: The study does not conduct formal scaling-law fits or broad sweeps over model sizes and compute. Several architecture-ablation results are shown only in figures, without numerical values or uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant architecture-ablation results left out. Scaling curves, downstream benchmark tables, and cited results are not rows for the versions tested here because they do not evaluate the relevant power-law or predictive claims.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss in parameters, tokens or compute. Only two model scales (760M- and 1.3B-FLOP-matched) are trained.
No fixed-compute sweep or fitted allocation. Hoffmann et al.'s FLOP formula is used only for matching.
No depth/width/shape variation at fixed parameter count. Only layer-type swaps in a hierarchical model.
Chinese, code and DNA runs report loss curves and final BPB/perplexity, but no power-law form is fitted.
Downstream accuracies are reported at two scales, but no predictive relation to scale or loss is tested.
No fitted exponents or analysis of fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label for V4 rests on layer-family swaps confounded by compression ratio and FLOPs. The 'supports' label rests on DNA models with unmatched parameter counts. Neither measures V4's shape claim, so both labels are dropped. Hoffmann et al.'s FLOP accounting is used only as a tool.

versions.untested_parts: Whether held-out loss follows a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Whether fits from smaller runs predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute sweep or fitted compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
The architecture ablations cover selected configurations, not a wide range of all depth, width, and architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study evaluates DNA, Chinese, and code modeling, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in those settings or other modalities and regimes.
Downstream tasks are evaluated, but the study does not test a predictive relationship between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, or sensitivity analysis of scaling-law fitting choices are reported.
